passage:
Hansa, sit with your Dada. You look the way I looked at fifteen, before my board exams.
Back then I would lie on the roof and think, if only I were six again. At six I flew kites all day, no books, no marks. Life was one long holiday, I told myself.
Then one evening my mother heard me moaning about it. She laughed. "Santosh, at six you were terrified of the dark. You cried every night the power went. And you begged to cross the road alone, and I never let you."
I had forgotten all of it. The kite days were true, but so was the dark.
I'm not saying exams are easy. I'm saying the old days weren't only kites. Now, show me which chapter is giving you trouble.

qa.q: What did Santosh's mother remind him he was scared of at six?
qa.a: The dark; he cried every night the power went.

qa.q: Why did fifteen-year-old Santosh long to be six again?
qa.a: With board exams pressing, the kite-flying days felt like one long holiday, a comfort compared with books and marks.

qa.q: How does Dada turn the memory into help for Hansa?
qa.a: He admits exams are hard, shows the past had its own fears, then moves straight to the difficult chapter, so the pressure gets tackled instead of escaped.

qa.q: What might Santosh's mother have been thinking when she laughed?
qa.a: She probably found it sweet and a little funny, since she remembered the nightly tears and the limits he had forgotten.

grounding: A grandfather recalls how, as a pressured teenager, he longed for carefree childhood until his mother reminded him of its fears and limits.

passage:
The power went out at nine, with Zeenat's project due at midnight and the laptop on eleven percent.
Zeenat lit the emergency lamp and flopped onto the bed. Across the room, Dilnaz, her eight-year-old sister, was happily colouring by lamplight.
"You're so lucky," Zeenat said. "I'd give anything to be eight. No deadlines. Just crayons and cartoons."
Dilnaz looked up. "I have a spelling test tomorrow. And I can't reach the top shelf. And you won't let me walk to the shop alone."
"That's different."
"And I'm scared of the dark," Dilnaz added, edging her lamp closer.
Zeenat remembered, suddenly, hiding under a blanket during power cuts at that age, heart thumping.
She sat up, opened the laptop, dimmed the screen, and typed the conclusion first.

qa.q: How much battery did Zeenat's laptop have when the power went out?
qa.a: Eleven percent, with the project due at midnight.

qa.q: Why does Zeenat wish she were eight again tonight?
qa.a: The deadline and the power cut make her feel trapped, so childhood looks like only crayons and cartoons, without the fears she once had. 😅

qa.q: What sensible step does Zeenat take once she stops wishing?
qa.a: She dims the screen to save battery and writes the conclusion first, working with the time and power she actually has.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see being eight?
qa.a: To Dilnaz, eight comes with its own worries: a spelling test, shelves out of reach, rules about the shop, and fear of the dark.

grounding: A teenager under deadline pressure envies her little sister's carefree age until the sister's own fears remind her what childhood was like.

passage:
Between school and evening coaching, Sonali had exactly forty minutes. She spent them on the floor of the Andheri flat, flipping through an old photo album.
There she was at five, chocolate on her chin, grinning at a birthday party. "Look at me," she said to Saurabh, her older brother, who was eating toast in the doorway. "Not a single worry. Why can't life be like that again?"
Saurabh leaned over and turned the page. Sonali, same age, howling on the edge of a swimming pool, clutching the rail.
"You screamed through every lesson that summer," he said. "And you cried when Mummy wouldn't let you go to the park without her."
Sonali frowned at the photo. She had forgotten the pool entirely.
"Still," she said, "it looks easier."
"Some of it was," Saurabh said. "Your bag's by the door."
She closed the album gently, not quite ready to put it away.

qa.q: What was Sonali doing in the swimming pool photo?
qa.a: Howling on the edge of a swimming pool, clutching the rail.

qa.q: Why does Sonali want life to be like it was at five?
qa.a: Squeezed between school and coaching, she longs for the carefree feeling in the birthday photo; the album is a comfort from the pressure.

qa.q: What could help Sonali with the pressure itself, not just the longing?
qa.a: Telling her family how packed her days feel and finding small breaks now, instead of looking for ease only in the past.

qa.q: How does Saurabh see Sonali's 'not a single worry' claim?
qa.a: Saurabh remembers the screaming at swimming lessons and the park rules, so he sees her early years as happy but not worry-free.

grounding: A busy teenager longs for her early childhood through photos, forgetting its fears until her brother turns the page.

passage: Last month, with three coaching tests a week, I kept opening old photos from when I was five: me in a yellow frock on our Hyderabad terrace, eating mango, laughing at nothing. I'd think, that girl had no worries at all. I missed her so much it hurt. Then, clearing my cupboard, I found my kindergarten drawing book. On one page, in wobbly letters, I had written "I am skared of thunder" beside a black cloud. Another page showed me alone at the gate, waiting for the school van, a tear drawn on my face. I sat on the floor for a long time. I told Aditi the next day. She said, "Maybe you miss being looked after, not being little." That felt right. I'm Zainab, and I still keep the mango photo on my wall, next to the thunder page.

qa.q: What had Zainab written beside the black cloud in the drawing book?
qa.a: "I am skared of thunder."

qa.q: Why did Zainab miss her five-year-old self so much during that month?
qa.a: The pressure of three coaching tests a week made the easy-looking photos feel like a lost comfort, so she saw only the laughter, not the fears.

qa.q: What did Zainab choose to do with the photo and the drawing, and why does it help?
qa.a: She kept the mango photo next to the thunder page, holding both the happy and the scared memories together.

qa.q: How did Aditi's view change the way Zainab saw her longing?
qa.a: Aditi suggested Zainab missed being looked after, not being little, which gave the feeling a clearer and kinder name.

grounding: A teenager under pressure remembers early childhood as carefree until she finds drawings that recall its fears.

passage: The power cut came at nine, two days before Bhavna's physics board exam. She lit a candle, stared at the formula sheet, and gave up. Ishita, revising in the same room for the same paper, heard her sigh. "I just want to be five again," Bhavna said. "No exams, no marks, just the swing in Nani's courtyard and mangoes." Ishita put down her pen. "You? At five? You screamed every time the lights went off. Your mum had to sleep with you." Bhavna laughed, then went quiet. She did remember that, a little: the dark stairwell, the thunder, being too small to reach the switch. "I guess I just remember the mangoes," she said. The candle flickered. She picked the sheet back up, holding it closer to the flame.

qa.q: When did the power cut happen?
qa.a: At nine, two days before Bhavna's physics board exam.

qa.q: Why does being five again feel so appealing to Bhavna?
qa.a: She feels pressured and tired before the board exam, so early childhood seems carefree, with only the swing and mangoes, and her old fears have faded from view.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do the next time the longing for childhood hits during revision?
qa.a: She could name what is heavy right now, take a short break, and plan one small task instead of comparing the present to a smoothed-over past.

qa.q: How does Ishita see Bhavna's wish to be five?
qa.a: Ishita remembers Bhavna screaming in the dark, so she sees the wish as leaving out the fears, and she gently reminds her with a joke.

grounding: Shows a teenager under exam pressure longing for a carefree childhood while forgetting how frightened she was then.

passage: Nazia found the old photo album while clearing the loft of their Hyderabad flat, the week her coaching schedule doubled. There she was at six in a frilly frock, grinning on a giant wheel. She sat on the dusty floor for twenty minutes. "Life was so easy then," she told her brother Farhan when he climbed up to help. "No tests, no ranks, nobody expecting anything." Farhan peered at the photo. "You cried because you were too short for that ride. Abba had to take the photo while it was standing still." Nazia snorted. "Rubbish." "And you were terrified of the school van driver's moustache." She looked again. Her grin did look a little stiff. Still, she slid the photo into her pencil box before going back to her maths notes.

qa.q: What did Nazia find while clearing the loft?
qa.a: She found the old photo album.

qa.q: Why did Nazia sit on the floor with the album for twenty minutes?
qa.a: She felt worn down by the doubled coaching schedule, and the photo made childhood look easy, so she felt a warm longing for a time when nobody expected anything of her.

qa.q: What small step could help Nazia with the coaching pressure itself?
qa.a: She could tell a parent or teacher how heavy the new schedule feels and ask for help planning breaks, rather than only escaping into old photos.

qa.q: How does Farhan see the photo differently from Nazia?
qa.a: Farhan remembers the tears about being too short and the fear of the van driver, so he sees the grin as less carefree than Nazia remembers.

grounding: Shows a teenager under study pressure longing for a childhood she remembers as easy while forgetting its fears and limits.

passage:
"Didi, remember when all I had to do was colour and nap?"
Alka looked up from her laptop. "Tanvir, you're seventeen. Nobody's making you nap."
"I'm serious. Class seven onwards it's just tests. When I was small nobody cared about my marks."
"You cared. You cried because Pinky got a gold star and you didn't."
"That's different."
"And you wouldn't sleep without the corridor light on until you were nine."
Tanvir groaned into a cushion. "Why do you remember everything?"
"Because I was the one who had to leave it on." She closed the laptop. "What's actually going on?"
"The mock results come out tomorrow."
"Okay. So being little looks good because tomorrow looks scary."
Tanvir didn't answer, but he stopped hiding his face.

qa.q: When do Tanvir's mock results come out?
qa.a: The mock results come out tomorrow.

qa.q: What is Tanvir worried about underneath his wish to be small again?
qa.a: He feels anxious about tomorrow's mock results, and that fear makes early childhood seem free of pressure.

qa.q: What did Alka do that helped Tanvir, and what could she add?
qa.a: She asked what was actually going on, which uncovered his worry; she could now help him plan how he will handle the results, whatever they are.

qa.q: If you were Alka, how would it feel to hear Tanvir call childhood easy?
qa.a: It might feel a bit funny and tender, since Alka remembers leaving the corridor light on for him and knows he had real fears back then too.

grounding: Shows a teenager longing for early childhood before a stressful result while forgetting the fears and jealousies of that time.

passage:
Last year, in the middle of board exams, I kept thinking about being five. No homework, no marks, just flying kites on the terrace with my cousin Jyoti and eating Nani's laddoos. I'd close my textbook and just want to go back.

One night I said this to Jyoti on the phone. She laughed. "Lokesh, you were scared of the dark till you were eight. You cried every day at school for a month. And you hated that you weren't allowed to go anywhere alone."

I had forgotten all of that. I only remembered the kites.

I think when things are hard now, my mind paints the past gold. It helped me to know that. Being five wasn't perfect. It was just far away.

qa.q: What does Lokesh remember doing at five?
qa.a: Flying kites on the terrace with Jyoti and eating Nani's laddoos.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh long to go back to being five during the exams?
qa.a: Lokesh felt stressed and pressured, so early childhood felt carefree and comforting, with its fears forgotten.

qa.q: How could Lokesh use this insight during the next stressful time?
qa.a: When longing for the past, Lokesh could remember that it had hard parts too, and take a short comforting break before returning to work.

qa.q: How does Jyoti see Lokesh's memories of being five?
qa.a: Jyoti seems amused and affectionate, remembering the fears and limits Lokesh forgot.

grounding: A teenager under exam pressure remembers early childhood as carefree and longs for it, forgetting its fears.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Monday.

Imran, class eleven, came to see me today. He said he felt tired of everything: tuition, coaching, family expectations. He kept talking about when he was small. "Life was so easy. I just played cricket all day in the lane."

I asked about his early years. His sister Hafsa, who walked him here, said quietly, "You were scared of the neighbour's dog. You hated going to school."

Imran laughed a little, surprised. "I forgot that."

I explained that when we feel pressured, the past can seem golden. We talked about small ways to make now easier. I'll meet him weekly, and with his permission I called his parents this evening to talk about the pressure he's under.

qa.q: What did Imran say he used to do all day when he was small?
qa.a: He played cricket all day in the lane.

qa.q: Why did Imran remember his childhood as easy?
qa.a: He felt tired and pressured by tuition and expectations, so the past seemed golden and comforting.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take?
qa.a: The counsellor explained why the past looks golden, planned weekly meetings and called his parents that evening, with his permission.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel walking Imran to the counsellor?
qa.a: Hafsa probably felt worried and caring, wanting her brother to get help.

grounding: A counsellor notes a teenager under pressure who remembers early childhood as carefree, forgetting its fears.

passage:
Wednesday night

Everything is too much. Physics test Friday, dance practice, and Mom and Dad keep asking about college. I just want to be seven again. Summer holidays at Grandma's, swimming in the lake, no worries at all.

Then I called Francis, my cousin who was there too. I said, "Remember how perfect those summers were?"

He said, "You were terrified of the lake. You wouldn't go past your knees. And you cried when Grandma made you eat okra."

I laughed so hard. I totally forgot.

Maybe the past wasn't perfect. Maybe I just miss feeling safe. Tomorrow I'll tell Mom I'm stressed instead of pretending I'm fine.

— Ankita

qa.q: What did Francis say Ankita was terrified of?
qa.a: The lake.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she wanted to be seven again?
qa.a: Ankita felt overwhelmed and stressed, and missed feeling safe, so childhood looked carefree.

qa.q: Is Ankita's plan for tomorrow a good one? Why?
qa.a: Yes, telling Mom about the stress lets a caring adult help, instead of hiding it.

qa.q: How might Francis feel after the call?
qa.a: Francis might feel amused and glad to have made Ankita laugh during a hard week.

grounding: A teenager under pressure remembers childhood as carefree and longs for it, forgetting its fears.

passage: Behind the family's kirana shop in Rajgarh, Anjali sat on a sack of rice with her physics book unopened. Between the shop counter, tuition and the entrance forms, every hour was spoken for. "Remember when we were small," she said to her cousin Disha, "and we spent whole days at Nani's farm, chasing goats? No worries at all." Disha, sorting coins, laughed softly. "You were terrified of the buffalo. And you cried whenever Nani made us come in before dark." Anjali paused. She had forgotten the buffalo. She had forgotten how small the world felt then, how she couldn't go anywhere without asking. Still, the ache stayed. "It feels lighter, in my head," she said. Disha nodded. "Maybe you need one light hour now, not the old days."

qa.q: Where did Anjali and Disha spend whole days as children?
qa.a: At Nani's farm.

qa.q: Why does Anjali still feel the ache after Disha reminds her?
qa.a: She feels overloaded and tired, so the farm days feel lighter in her head; comfort and loss colour the memory even when she recalls the buffalo.

qa.q: What could help Anjali now?
qa.a: As Disha suggests, carve out one light hour in the present rather than longing for the past, and perhaps talk to the family about the load.

qa.q: How does Disha see Anjali's longing?
qa.a: Disha remembers the fears and rules too, but responds with understanding rather than just correcting her.

grounding: A pressured teenager remembers childhood as carefree and forgets its fears and limits.

passage: Rania's alarm went off at five-thirty again, for the extra maths class before school in Amman. On the bus she scrolled through old family photos: herself as a little girl on the beach at Aqaba, sticky with ice cream, grinning. "Everything was so easy then," she said to her little brother Siddiq, who was half asleep against her shoulder. "Easy?" he mumbled. "Mama says you screamed every time a wave touched you. And you weren't allowed past the rocks." Rania looked closer at the photo. In the corner, barely visible, was her own hand gripping Baba's sleeve. She had forgotten the fear. But she still wanted, badly, to be back in that picture, where nobody asked about marks.

qa.q: Why does Rania long to be back in the photo?

qa.q: What small step could help Rania with the present pressure?

qa.q: How does Siddiq see Rania's easy childhood?
qa.a: Siddiq, repeating what Mama says, sees it more realistically: she was scared of the waves and not allowed past the rocks.

grounding: A pressured teenager longs for a carefree childhood, forgetting the fears and limits that were also there.

passage:
In the coaching centre's counselling room in Kota, the ceiling fan pushed hot May air around. Joseph stared at a poster of a beach.
"I just wish I was eight again," he said. "No tests, no ranks. Just cycling and mangoes. Everything was easy."
Shalini Ma'am, the counsellor, nodded. "That sounds lovely. What else do you remember about being eight?"
He smiled. Then the smile slipped. "I was scared of the dark. I slept in Amma's room till I was ten. And I cried every morning before school because of that boy who took my tiffin."
"So not only easy."
"No." He laughed a little. "I forgot that part."
"The pressure now is real," she said. "Let's also talk about what would help this week."

qa.q: What did Joseph say he was scared of at eight?
qa.a: He was scared of the dark.

qa.q: Why does being eight feel so easy to Joseph right now?
qa.a: Under the weight of tests and ranks he feels tired and longs for comfort, so his memory keeps the cycling and mangoes and drops the fears.

qa.q: What did Shalini Ma'am do well?
qa.a: She let Joseph find the harder parts of childhood himself with one open question, without arguing, and then turned to real help for this week's pressure.

qa.q: What would change if Shalini Ma'am had just said, "Childhood wasn't easy either"?
qa.a: Joseph might have felt dismissed and defensive, and missed noticing for himself what he had forgotten.

grounding: Shows a teenager under pressure remembering early childhood as carefree and forgetting its fears.
